rules.title: Multi-employer worksites: four kinds of employer can be cited
rules.plain_english: On a jobsite with more than one employer, Cal/OSHA can cite four kinds of employer for the same hazard: the one whose workers were exposed, the one who created it, the one in control of site safety (usually the GC), and the one whose job it was to fix it.

definitions.exposing: employer whose employees were exposed to the hazard
definitions.creating: employer who actually created the hazard
definitions.controlling: employer responsible, by contract or through actual practice, for safety and health conditions on the worksite (authority to ensure correction)
definitions.correcting: employer who had the responsibility for actually correcting the hazard

rules.verbatim_quote: On multi-employer worksites, both construction and non-construction, citations may be issued only to the following categories of employers when the Division has evidence that an employee was exposed to a hazard in violation of any requirement enforceable by the Division:
rules.notes: Cal/OSHA Compliance Manual Ch. 14-B notes that one employer may fit more than one category (e.g., creating and controlling). 336.10 history: filed 12/1/97, effective 12/31/97; the Compliance Manual (section III) says 'Beginning in January of 2000, Labor Code Section 6400 and 8 CCR Section 336.10 now permit the Division to cite' creating, controlling and correcting employers. rules.title: Controlling employer (usually the GC) can be cited for subs' hazards
rules.plain_english: The employer responsible for site safety, by contract or by how it actually runs the job, is the 'controlling employer'. Cal/OSHA can cite it for a hazard on the site even if none of its own workers were exposed.
rules.applies_to: General contractors, construction managers and any employer with contractual or actual authority over jobsite safety
rules.verbatim_quote: (c) The employer who was responsible, by contract or through actual practice, for safety and health conditions on the worksite; i.e., the employer who had the authority for ensuring that the hazardous condition is corrected (the controlling employer); or

rules.title: Controlling the schedule or key information can make you the controlling employer

rules.title: Exposing employer is not cited only if all five defenses are met
rules.plain_english: A sub whose workers were exposed to someone else's hazard avoids a citation only if it did not create the hazard, had no responsibility or authority to fix it, could not fix it, told the responsible employer (or they knew), and took feasible steps to protect and instruct its own workers (including pulling them off the job for an extreme hazard).

rules.applies_to: Subcontractors and other exposing employers on multi-employer worksites
rules.verbatim_quote: Prior to issuing any citation to an exposing employer, the Division shall first determine whether available information indicates that the employer meets each of the defenses listed below. If the Division concludes that all five defenses have been met, the citation shall not be issued.
rules.notes: Compliance Manual Ch. 14-B, IV says that if the employer appeals a determination that the defense does not apply, 'it is the employer's burden to demonstrate that the defense applies.' Practical takeaway: subs should notify the GC in writing of hazards they did not create.

rules.title: Definition: confined space (3-part test)
rules.plain_english: A confined space is any space big enough for a worker to get fully inside, with limited or restricted ways in or out, and not designed for people to stay in continuously.

limited or restricted means for entry and exit
not designed for continuous employee occupancy

rules.verbatim_quote: Confined space means a space that: (1) Is large enough and so configured that an employee can bodily enter it; (2) Has limited or restricted means for entry and exit; and (3) Is not designed for continuous employee occupancy.

rules.title: Definition: permit-required confined space (any 1 of 4 hazards)
rules.plain_english: A confined space becomes a permit-required space if it has, or could have, a hazardous atmosphere, material that could engulf a worker, a shape that could trap or suffocate someone, or any other serious safety or health hazard.

any_one_of: inwardly converging walls or downward-sloping tapering floor
any other recognized serious safety or health hazard

rules.applies_to: Construction employers whose employees work at a worksite with one or more confined spaces (not excavations, tunnels, diving or pressurized work)
rules.verbatim_quote: Permit-required confined space (permit space) means a confined space that has one or more of the following characteristics: (1) Contains or has a potential to contain a hazardous atmosphere; (2) Contains a material that has the potential for engulfing an entrant; (3) Has an internal configuration such that an entrant could be trapped or asphyxiated by inwardly converging walls or by a floor which slopes downward and tapers to a smaller cross-section; or (4) Contains any other recognized serious safety or health hazard.
